chunks: Characterizing measurement error. The question: How do you characterize measurement error? What can you do with that information?
Every measurement is wrong by some amount. Characterizing the error means measuring a known reference many times and splitting the mistakes into two kinds.
Bias is the average offset, the same every time. Random error is the scatter around that average.
The two kinds respond to different fixes, and combining several error sources takes a special rule.
Imagine measuring a table with a tape measure that has stretched a little, using shaky hands. The stretch makes every reading wrong by the same proportion, which is bias.
The shaky hands make each reading a bit different, which is random error. Measuring ten times and averaging calms the shaking, but the stretched tape still gives the wrong answer.
Only checking the tape against a known ruler, which is calibration, fixes that.
The whole curve is shifted right of the true value by the bias (12 millivolts), while its width is the noise (20 millivolts).
Calibration slides the curve left onto zero; averaging makes the curve narrower; neither does the other's job.
Bias: the average error, repeatable and correctable by calibration. Random error (noise): scatter around the average, which averaging reduces.
Standard deviation: the typical size of the scatter of single readings. Standard error of the mean: the standard deviation divided by the square root of the number of readings.
It tells how well you know the average. Root-sum-square (RSS): combining independent errors by squaring each, adding, and taking the square root.
A sensor measures a 5. 000 volts reference 100 times. The mean is 5. 012 volts and the standard deviation is 20 millivolts. The bias is plus 12 millivolts.
The standard error is 20 divided by the square root of 100, which is 2 millivolts. So the bias is about 12 plus or minus 4 millivolts (two standard errors), clearly not zero.
A single reading still scatters by 20 millivolts.
For combining, independent errors of 3 millivolts and 4 millivolts give 5 millivolts by RSS, not 7 millivolts, since independent errors partly cancel. That is the whole idea.
"I take many readings against a reference and compute error as reading minus truth. The mean is the bias, which I can calibrate out.
The standard deviation is the random error, which averaging reduces as one over root N until drift sets a floor.
I check the histogram for Gaussian shape and outliers and plot error against time and temperature. Independent sources combine in quadrature into a total uncertainty.
I then use that to set calibration, specs and guard bands, and the measurement noise in a Kalman filter."
Quick check. Which kind of error can be removed by calibration but NOT by averaging?
